extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York; readers and voters engaged in the ratification debate over the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Persuasive 18th-century political essays arguing for or against provisions of the proposed U.S. Constitution, addressing citizens and state electorates. These essays explain, justify, and rebut constitutional design choices (militia, taxation, federal/state powers) through reasoned argument and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal regulation of the militia
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union should be empowered "to provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the militia, and for governing such part of them as may be employed in the service of the United States."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: If a well-regulated militia is the most natural defense of a free country, it ought to be under the regulation and at the disposal of the body charged with national security. Federal control over militia organization and deployment reduces the inducement to standing armies and enables the Union to command militia aid in emergencies, thereby avoiding different, more dangerous military forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: States retain appointment and training authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision reserves "to the States respectively the appointment of the officers, and the authority of training the militia according to the discipline prescribed by Congress."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This division (federal organization/policy; state appointment and training) is presented as a constitutional safeguard: federal regulation with state control of officers helps prevent federal domination of the militia and preserves local influence and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to require citizen assistance (posse comitatus implied)
rubrics_metrics.description: A right to pass all laws NECESSARY AND PROPER to execute declared powers includes requiring the assistance of citizens (POSSE COMITATUS) to officers entrusted with execution of those laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rebuts the objection that the Constitution lacks authority to call out citizen aid; the necessary-and-proper clause implies power to enlist citizen assistance in law execution without implying exclusive reliance on military force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training the entire militia is impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: The project of disciplining all the militia of the United States is as futile as it would be injurious; tolerable expertness in military movements requires time and practice and cannot be imposed on the whole populace frequently without severe economic burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy recommendation: avoid obliging the mass of citizens to frequent drills. Practical compromise: ensure citizens are properly armed and equiped and assemble them once or twice a year to check preparedness rather than continuous compulsory drilling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a select, well-trained militia corps
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a select corps of moderate extent, upon principles that will really fit them for service in case of need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By circumscribing training to a moderate, select body, the government can have an excellent, well-trained militia ready for the field; this lessens reliance on standing armies and provides a credible check on potential military usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia as substitute and check on standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: A large body of citizens, little if at all inferior to a standing army in discipline and use of arms, who stand ready to defend their rights, is the best substitute and security against a standing army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: An armed, trained citizen militia reduces the need for and the danger of a permanent army; it also makes any attempt at despotism by a standing army self-defeating, as the populace would be hostile to instruments of usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government must possess general power of taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be interwoven in the frame of the government a general power of taxation, in one shape or another, to provide for support of national forces, payment of national debts, the national civil list, and all matters calling for disbursements from the national treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revenue is the vital principle of the body politic; a complete power to procure a regular and adequate supply of money, as far as community resources permit, is indispensable. Without it the government risks being plundered, impotent, or perishing from atrophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject dependence on requisitions/quotas from states
rubrics_metrics.description: The requisition/quota system is fallacious: requiring the national government to depend on separate state contributions is unreliable and has produced the Confederation's feebleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: the national government should be empowered to raise its own revenues by ordinary modes of taxation, since states' intermediacy has historically produced deficient supplies and discord between national and state governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between internal and external taxation is unworkable
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserving INTERNAL taxation to the states and conceding to the Union only EXTERNAL taxation (duties on imports) would violate the maxim that every power ought to be in proportion to its object and would leave the general government in tutelage to the states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customs duties alone cannot meet present and future exigencies (debt, necessary establishments). Therefore the federal government requires ordinary taxation powers, not just imposts, to be effective and creditworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxing power should be commensurate with national necessities
rubrics_metrics.description: As duties of national defense and security involve provisions for casualties and dangers without possible limits, the power of making that provision ought to know no other bounds than the exigencies of the nation and the resources of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: the scope of revenue-raising authority must match the indefinite or evolving needs of the nation; hence vesting an unconfined power of taxation in the national government is justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliable taxation underpins credit and war finance
rubrics_metrics.description: Without authority to create new funds by taxation, the government would be driven to divert appropriated funds or seek loans under ruinous terms; public credit depends on assurance of steady taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical point: in war modern states must borrow; lenders will only trust a government able to raise revenues itself. A government's ability to borrow on reasonable terms depends on credible, autonomous taxation power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal taxing power enables borrowing and fiscal confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of creating new funds upon new objects of taxation would enable the national government to borrow as far as necessities require and assure both foreigners and citizens that its engagements are trustworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: the combination of taxation power and borrowing capacity secures national credit and avoids dependence on states for fiscal fulfillment.

rubrics_metrics.name: State taxation sovereignty preserved except constitutional exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual States should possess independent and uncontrollable authority to raise their own revenues for their own wants; under the plan, with sole exception of duties on imports/exports, they retain that authority unless the Constitution exclusively delegates it to the Union or the federal and state powers would be repugnant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarification: exclusive delegation to the Union exists where Constitution expressly grants exclusive authority, or grants in one instance and prohibits states in another, or where concurrent state authority would be absolutely contradictory or repugnant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections founded on usurpation should examine government structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns about usurpation ought to be referred to the composition and structure of the government, not to the mere nature or extent of its powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological guidance: avoid speculative fears of usurpation as a ground for limiting enumerated powers; instead analyze structural safeguards, the manner of formation, and accountability of the governmental organs to the people.
